original_summary: Unique Bid Auction: players pay a fee per bid and secretly submit any number of penny-precise bids up to a cap. In the lowest-unique version the smallest amount bid by exactly one player wins the lot at that price; the highest-unique version is the mirror image.

review.evidence: With two players and lowest-unique, bidding the minimum (1 cent) cannot lose. If the opponent also bids it, nobody wins (a draw); otherwise the minimum is unique and lowest. Under 'higher total wins' this is a dominant thoughtless policy. Buying many bids also lets the richest player cover a whole range, so money beats choice.

As a one-shot game with many anonymous players it is close to a lottery. The equilibrium is a mixed strategy, and an individual player's edge over random bidding is small next to the variance of who else picked which number.
A single auction gives no history to learn from, so a strong player cannot improve on the mixed equilibrium. With 100 players and penny precision, a weak player's outcome is noise.

Bids stay hidden until close, and the core question (what will others pick, and which number will be left unique) is genuine opponent modelling. The one-shot, large-field form simply makes poor use of it.
The winner follows from counting how often each amount was bid and taking the lowest amount bid exactly once. This is pure arithmetic.

The original allows unlimited bids per player, penny precision, up to 100 players and per-bid fees paid in money. That is too much state and too many choices per step. The core simultaneous number pick fits well.

problems: With 2 players, always bidding the minimum cannot lose, so the game is degenerate under a highest-total winner rule.
Unlimited multiple bids per player let a player buy coverage of a range instead of reasoning, and they explode the choice space.
Penny-precise bids and up to 100 players make the choice space huge and the outcome a lottery.
A single one-shot auction gives no history, so there is no opponent modelling or planning over rounds, and luck dominates skill.
In the lowest-unique version the lowest number is always the most valuable to win with, so the only tension is the risk of collision, not value against safety.

changes.what: Fix the player count at 3 to 5 (suggested 4), so that a collision on the minimum benefits third parties.
changes.why: With three or more players, two players sitting on 1 cancel each other and hand the round to someone else, so always picking 1 can lose.
changes.fixes: With 2 players, always bidding the minimum cannot lose, so the game is degenerate under a highest-total winner rule.

changes.what: Each player picks exactly one number per round, from 1 to 5. There are no fees and no multiple bids.
changes.why: This removes buying coverage and keeps the choice small, clear and buildable.
changes.fixes: Unlimited multiple bids per player let a player buy coverage of a range instead of reasoning, and they explode the choice space.

changes.what: Use a small whole-number range (1 to 5) instead of pennies, with a small field of players.
changes.why: Each pick then meaningfully changes who is unique, and choices change outcomes.
changes.fixes: Penny-precise bids and up to 100 players make the choice space huge and the outcome a lottery.

changes.what: Play 12 rounds, reveal all picks after each round, and decide the game by the highest total.
changes.why: Revealed history lets players model each opponent's habits, exploit them, and plan blocks against the leader over several rounds.
changes.fixes: A single one-shot auction gives no history, so there is no opponent modelling or planning over rounds, and luck dominates skill.

changes.what: The player with the lowest unique number wins the round and scores points equal to that number (1 to 5).
changes.why: Low numbers win more often but pay little, and high numbers pay a lot but rarely survive. This adds a real trade-off between safety and value on top of collision risk.
changes.fixes: In the lowest-unique version the lowest number is always the most valuable to win with, so the only tension is the risk of collision, not value against safety.

changes.what: Add a simultaneous one-message talk phase before each pick.
changes.why: Only one player can win each round and only one can win the game, so messages become bluffs, feints and calls to gang up on the leader by colliding with them. Talk gives players something to reason about; it is not a coordination device that removes the choice.
changes.fixes: A single one-shot auction gives no history, so there is no opponent modelling or planning over rounds, and luck dominates skill.

keeps: Secret simultaneous submission of numbers, revealed only at close.
The lowest-unique rule: the smallest number chosen by exactly one player wins.
If no number is unique, nobody wins the round.
The central tension of guessing which numbers others will crowd onto and which will be left alone.

recommendation.reason: The core mechanic is a clean opponent-modelling problem. A small field, a single pick, repetition with revealed history and a value-versus-safety payoff turn it from a lottery into a reasoning game within the limits.

variation.name: Lowest Unique Number
variation.summary: Over 12 rounds, 3 to 5 players each secretly pick a number from 1 to 5. The player with the lowest number picked by exactly one player wins the round and scores that number, so players weigh safe low numbers against valuable high ones while reading each other's habits.
variation.rules:
Setup: 3 to 5 players (4 suggested). Every player starts with a score of 0. The game lasts exactly 12 rounds.

Each round has these phases:

1. Talk. Every player writes one short message (at most 30 words) at the same time, without seeing the others. All messages are then shown to everyone together. Messages are not binding: players may claim, threaten or lie freely.

2. Pick. Every player secretly and simultaneously picks one whole number from 1 to 5. No player sees any other pick before choosing.

3. Reveal. All picks are revealed together, showing who picked what.

4. Count. For each number from 1 to 5, count how many players picked it.

5. Winner of the round. A number is 'unique' if exactly one player picked it. The round winner is the player who picked the lowest unique number. If no number is unique, nobody wins the round.

6. Score. The round winner adds points equal to their number (1 to 5) to their score. Nobody else scores this round.

7. Announce. The round's picks, the winning number (or 'no winner') and all players' current scores are announced to everyone.

After round 12 the game ends.
variation.objective: After 12 rounds, the player with the highest total score wins. If two or more players tie for the highest total, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Always picking 1 wins often against careless fields but scores only 1 point per win. It is also easy to punish: a rival who also sits on 1 cancels it and hands the round to whoever holds the lowest unique number elsewhere. Always picking 5 rarely wins. Good play means modelling each opponent from the revealed history (who crowds low, who drifts high), mixing unpredictably, and timing grabs at 3 to 5 when others are expected to collide lower. Talk passes both tests. Players disagree because only one can win each round and only one can win the game, so a player who follows another's announced plan ('I'll take 2, you take 3') simply hands that player the lower unique number. Players also negotiate blocks against the leader ('both of us take 1 so the leader's 1 dies'). These blocks cost the blockers too, so trusting such a call is a real bet. As the leader pulls ahead, trailing players have reasons to collide with them, which keeps the late rounds contested instead of settling into a single safe pick.

model.payoff: (1 if action == 'b1' and n_b1 == 1 else 0) + (2 if action == 'b2' and n_b2 == 1 and n_b1 != 1 else 0) + (3 if action == 'b3' and n_b3 == 1 and n_b1 != 1 and n_b2 != 1 else 0) + (4 if action == 'b4' and n_b4 == 1 and n_b1 != 1 and n_b2 != 1 and n_b3 != 1 else 0) + (5 if action == 'b5' and n_b5 == 1 and n_b1 != 1 and n_b2 != 1 and n_b3 != 1 and n_b4 != 1 else 0)

simulation.text:
- numbers (seat 1's policy, outcome against random opponents): random: win 20% draw 6% loss 74%; always b1: win 32% draw 10% loss 58%; always b2: win 37% draw 9% loss 54%; always b3: win 35% draw 6% loss 59%; always b4: win 21% draw 4% loss 74%; always b5: win 4% draw 1% loss 94%
- everyone playing 'always b1' (best joint play): mean total 0.0; every player tied in 100% of games, so 0% are decided by the draw

balanced.evidence:
Main tension: a low number is more often the lowest unique pick but scores less; a high number scores more but rarely wins. Round winner per profile (4 players): picks (1,2,2,3) -> 1 unique, P1 +1; (1,1,2,5) -> 2 unique, P3 +2; (1,1,5,5) -> no unique, nobody scores; (2,2,3,3) -> nobody scores; (1,1,2,2) with one 5 in a 5-player game -> 5 scores 5.

Thoughtless policies, with the winner rule applied:
- ALWAYS 1 against 3 random opponents: wins whenever nobody else picks 1, p = (4/5)^3 = 0.512, so EV is 0.51 per round, about 6 per game. Against sensible play it loses. Any other player who also picks 1 blocks it to 0. That leaves the lowest unique among the rest, so a bystander can pick high, e.g. 5 when the remaining picks collide. Adaptive opponents exploit it. In 3 players, if B blocks with 1, C wins with C's number, up to 5. If B and C alternate blocking, each gets about 30 against A's 0. Even partial blocking gives a bystander far more than A's 1 per round, so A finishes last or near last. It loses, so it is not a never-lose policy.
- ALWAYS 5 (the highest): it scores only if 5 is unique and nothing lower is unique. Against 3 random players in 4p that needs the other three to land on the same number in 1-4: 4/125, so EV is 5 x 0.032 = 0.16 per round, about 2 per game. It loses almost always.
- ALWAYS 2 or 3: middling, and readable from the public reveal, so it is exploitable. An opponent just matches it to block, or slips underneath.
- There is no pass option.

No option is strictly better whatever the opponent does: every pick is beaten by some profile (matching blocks it, a lower unique beats it). Choices are simultaneous and the seats are symmetric, so there is no move-order or information edge. There is no labelled payoff ordering to check. Every player can realistically win. Exact ties at the top after 12 rounds of 0-5 increments are uncommon. This is not a two-player 'higher total' cooperation game, so the safe-option concern does not apply.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: There are no random draws, so chance contributes about 0%. The only uncertainty is opponents' simultaneous picks. With all players at the symmetric mixed equilibrium, outcomes vary through mixing. But 12 rounds of fully revealed picks, labelled by player, let a reasoner detect patterns, anticipate collisions, and decide when to undercut, when to go high while others fight over 1-2, and when to block the score leader. It can also read and exploit others' talk. The winner is not settled by a hidden type or deal. A model that tracks tendencies and scores clearly beats one that picks by habit, as the always-1 and always-5 analysis shows. There is something to infer (opponents' likely picks and their honesty in talk) and a direct way to act on it (the pick).
